title: Fewest Splits to Make a Row Non-Decreasing
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers. In one move you pick any element and replace it, in its place, with two positive integers that add up to it. For example, [4, 9] can become [4, 2, 7] or [1, 3, 9].

Return the fewest moves needed to make the array non-decreasing (every element is at most the one after it).

examples.why: The 3 at the end cannot change. 9 must become 3 + 3 + 3 (2 moves), and then 4 must become 2 + 2 (1 move): [2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3].
10 needs 3 pieces of at most 4. Make them 3 + 3 + 4, not 2 + 4 + 4: the smallest piece stays 3, so the 3 in front needs no move.

hints: The last element never needs splitting: splitting it only makes the end smaller. So work from right to left.
Going right to left, keep a cap: the value the current element's pieces must not exceed. An element v > cap needs at least ⌈v / cap⌉ pieces. Is using more pieces ever better?
Use exactly k = ⌈v / cap⌉ pieces and make them as even as possible. The smallest piece is ⌊v / k⌋, and that becomes the new cap for the elements to the left.

explain.intuition:
The last element should stay whole: any split only lowers the end and makes everything before it harder. So scan from right to left, keeping a cap that the current element's pieces must not exceed (its right neighbor's first piece).

If v ≤ cap, keep it whole: it becomes the new cap. Otherwise you need at least k = ⌈v / cap⌉ pieces, costing k − 1 moves. Two choices remain, and both have a greedy answer. Use exactly k pieces, because more pieces cost more and only shrink the smallest piece. And split as evenly as possible, because the elements to the left only care about the first (smallest) piece, and the largest possible smallest piece with k parts is ⌊v / k⌋. In [3, 10, 4], 10 split as 3 + 3 + 4 leaves a cap of 3 and the 3 in front is fine; 2 + 4 + 4 would force another move.
steps: For i from n − 2 down to 0, let v = nums[i].
Otherwise: k = ⌈v / cap⌉, add k − 1 to moves, and set cap = ⌊v / k⌋.
pitfalls: Splitting into pieces of size cap plus a remainder. The remainder becomes a tiny cap and causes extra moves to the left.
Scanning left to right. You cannot know how small an early element must get until you have seen what follows it.
Using 32-bit integers for the count. It can reach about 10¹⁴.

solutions.title: Try every piece count (memoized)
solutions.idea: Right to left, for an element v with cap c, try every number of pieces from ⌈v / c⌉ to v, each giving a best possible new cap ⌊v / k⌋. Take the cheapest. It confirms that the fewest pieces is always best.
solutions.time: O(n · V²) for values up to V

solutions.title: Greedy from the right, even splits
solutions.idea: Use the fewest pieces that fit under the cap, split as evenly as possible, and pass the smallest piece left as the new cap.

followups: Return the final array as well. How large can it get, and can you describe it without listing it?
Allow a move to split an element into any number of parts at once. What changes?
lcTitle: Minimum Replacements to Sort the Array
